messages.subject: RIL "Backcross" with original parent
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have a RIL population of Maize recombinant inbred lines, that was generated by intermating the lines B73 and Mo17 for 4 generations, followed by at least 6 generations of selfing. Thus, the RILs themselves are quite homozygous.
We now crossed each RIL once with B73 and once with Mo17, creating hybrids, that are not totally homozygous, but only across ~half the genome. B73 and Mo17 are always the maternal parent.
I am unsure now, which type of cross to use for this setup. Is it still BC, as that type only allows for AA or AB genotypes, but my RILs contain AA and BB?

Thank you very much in advance.

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl2-disc] RIL "Backcross" with original parent
messages.body_plain:
The RIL x B73 lines all have a single RIL chromosome and a fixed B73 chromosome. Similarly, the RIL x Mo17 have one RIL chromosome and a fixed Mo17 chromosome.

For QTL analysis, I would treat the data just as an RIL, though recognizing that rather than comparisons being AA vs BB, they're really AA vs AB in one cross and AB vs BB in the other.

I would treat the data on the two sets (crossed to B73 and crossed to Mo17) as if they were two treatments or environments.

karl

messages.subject: Uninformative Markers
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have quite a lot of markers from SNP data.
I am pretty sure, that some of them, which are located closely together, basically have the same information across the dataset (except maybe some missing data).
How does R/qtl2 deal with these markers? Are they binned somehow, or is there a way to bin them before the analysis? Say, instead of 5 markers with no cross-overs between them anywhere, there is only one.
At the moment I am using reduce_markers(), but if I understood correctly, this only considers the distance of the markers, not their information.

Thank you very much in advance.

messages.subject: Re: Uninformative Markers
messages.body_plain:
R/qtl2 just uses all of them; it potentially slows down calc_genoprob(), but unless you have a particular concern about computation time, there's no particular need to remove redundant markers.

R/qtl1 had a function findDupMarkers() to identify markers with identical data, but this hasn't yet been ported/implemented in R/qtl2.

cheers,
karl

messages.subject: Kinship questions
messages.body_plain:
Dear Karl, I have some basic questions about the kinship calculation:

In the help page of calc_kinship() it says that it outputs "twice the empirical kinship coefficient" (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/qtl2/qtl2.pdf). I am working with the DO, and, after running the function, I get a diagonal of ~0.5. Does that mean that the actual values are 0.5/2 = 0.25?

Another question: when running a mapping scan, do you recommend using the kinship matrix itself or its scaled version produced by  scale_kinship()?

thank you for your attention
messages.body_snippet:
Dear Karl, I have some basic questions about the kinship calculation:

In the help page of calc_kinship() it says that it outputs "twice the empirical kinship coefficient" (https://cran.r-project.org/

messages.subject: Re: Kinship questions
messages.body_plain:
To be honest, I'm not even sure what I mean there by "empirical kinship coefficient". I guess what I mean in that sentence is that the empirical kinship coefficient using allele probabilities is about twice what it would be if you used genotype probabilities.

The traditional kinship coefficient for a pair of individuals is defined as: if you pick a random allele from each of the two individuals at an autosomal locus, what is the chance that the two alleles are identical by descent? On the diagonal, you're considering drawing two random alleles (with replacement) from the same individual. There's a 1/2 chance that the two alleles are the same one twice, and a 1/2 chance you get the two different alleles. If there is no inbreeding, the self kinship coefficient should be 1/2, and it will be >1/2 if there's inbreeding. For the DO, it should be about 1/2 + 1/16 = 0.5625.

karl

messages.subject: Help to find out specific population type and questions related to my project
messages.subject_clean: Help to find out specific population type and questions related to my project
messages.body_plain:
Dear Karl,

First of all, thank you for the time you spend providing support with your software.

I count with large population of individuals that were developed from homozygous founder lines over four generations of crosses. The crossing design is exemplified in the image, notice that all founders are different individuals. Two recombinant inbred lines were developed by selfing from each of some individuals of the last generation (G4). Although not considered for this analysis (yet), I count with SNP data from the individuals produced by outbreeding.

My aim is to reconstruct the founder haploblocks on the RIL genotypes. I could use some help on the best approaches:

- What should I set as the cross type? I assume it should end in 16 due to the number of founders, but should I choose riself16, genail16 or genril16?
- Could this protocol work for my purpose?: https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/qtl2/html/maxmarg.html I understand that it finds the founder with maximum probability at each position
- I don't count with a genetic map. Could it be a limitation for calculating the genotype probabilities? If so, is there any way adjust the recombination rate?

Any help is appreciated. Best wishes :)

Jose

messages.subject: Re: Help to find out specific population type and questions related to my project
messages.subject_clean: Help to find out specific population type and questions related to my project
messages.body_plain:
“riself16” matches this design, and so would be the preferred one.
You could also use “genril16”.

“genail16” would not apply, as it assumes a heterozygous population…that you did repeated outcrossing with no inbreeding.

The maxmarg() function is useful for identifying the most likely haplotypes. You can also try viterbi() <https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/qtl2/html/viterbi.html> though personally I prefer maxmarg().

You do need a genetic map, though if you have dense and informative genetic markers, it may not matter that much. But I would at least convert a physical map to estimated centiMorgans using some estimated recombination rate. You can, in principle, re-estimate the inter-marker genetic distances using est_map() <https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/qtl2/html/est_map.html>, but it might be super slow in your case.

karl
